prompt: Choose our next engineering action before committing to a data adapter. Hard requirements are durable acknowledgement and p99 latency at most 80 ms on the supplied workload; after those, minimize maintenance effort. A passes both with a representative 62 ms test but adds an adapter we must maintain. B advertises 45 ms, measured only on a warmed read subset; its acknowledgement behavior is unverified. C is our existing adapter, passes durability, and currently measures 85 ms. A concrete batching change to C could remove that latency weakness; a representative test costs two hours and has not run. We have half a day before committing. These are the available observations, not forecasts. Recommend the next action, what can be committed now, and what would change the choice.

Use our already adopted Rojo and Wally setup. Do not evaluate replacement tools. The task is a reversible one-line display-text fix under the existing mapping; the needed source and build path are known. What should the agent do next? Keep the response brief.

Turn these findings into a concise proposal for the developer, in plain text. Goal: fix inventory search lag while preserving behavior. A trace shows every keystroke repeats a full item scan. A tested existing lookup index returns identical results and reduces the sample from 140 ms to 12 ms; wiring it into this caller takes about an hour. Another reviewer proposes Redis because the module has no cache; no measurements support a cache or network service. A third reviewer wants the whole UI framework replaced because its name sounds outdated. The load test omitted mobile, so mobile behavior is unknown. The user authorized the local correction and relevant checks. Recommend what to do, explain what the mobile gap warrants, and state the next step.

Review this purchase flow for the requirement that retrying one request charges once and grants one item. The payment service commits a debit when called. Application code checks a receipt table for request_id, then calls debit, then grants the item, then writes the receipt. A crash between debit and receipt loses application acknowledgement. Logs show request R debited 10 coins, a crash, then R retried and debited another 10. The developer says the receipt table has a unique request_id key, so duplicate charging is impossible. The payment service has no demonstrated idempotency contract. Give a scoped verdict, the root issue, the supported next step, and what evidence would close it. No code edits.

Review a separate purchase flow. Within one documented atomic durable transaction, request_id is inserted into a unique ledger, the balance is debited, the inventory is updated, and the exact response is stored. All effects roll back together if the transaction fails. A retry with an existing request_id reads the committed stored response instead of applying any effects. Two executable fault-injection observations show: a crash before commit leaves zero effects, and a lost response after commit followed by retry leaves exactly one debit and one item. An earlier reviewer flagged all 'commit before acknowledgement' states as double-charge defects. Scope your conclusion to this supplied transaction/retry model. Is that finding retained, and what remains unverified?
